content:
What happens when “Euro summer” meets “island time?” The two laid-back, beachy vibes meet in liquid form in Italy’s island liqueurs. Off the coast of the boot, Italy has hundreds of islands from large to small, scattered across the Mediterranean. Similar to the cultural centers across the mainland, many of them produce their own beverages by sourcing local ingredients and steeping them in neutral alcohols. Tasting through these liqueurs can give consumers a glimpse of the islands’ terroirs.

Aperitifs like Aperol might dominate the Italian — and global — cocktail scene right now, but the islands offer a suite of regional products, from local amari to botanical liqueurs that showcase local fruits and flowers. While they can get the Spritz treatment, we encourage the liqueur-curious to sip these spirits straight, just as locals would.

From the scenic lemon groves off of the Amalfi Coast to the sulfuric slopes of Sicily’s Mount Etna, here are four Italian island liqueurs to know.

Capri: Limoncello

Today, tourists across the Amalfi Coast encounter dozens of tchotchke shops full of pastel-yellow limoncello handles and shooters, but the spirit has much more traditional roots. Coming from Capri, an island off the coast where lemon groves with massive, egg-shaped fruit are plentiful, the spirit first came about in the early 20th century. It is made by steeping lemon peels in a high-proof base alcohol and mixing it with sugar and water. (The recipe is so simple that you can make it at home.) With citrus peels headlining the flavor profile, the sweet lemon liqueur can lean into bitter territory, but it can also be sessionable, depending on how much sugar and water is added. The ABV for a typical bottle falls between 25 to 32 percent. Limoncello is traditionally served ice-cold in small glasses to be slowly sipped as a digestivo.

Ischia: Rucolino

As some English-speaking countries refer to arugula as “rocket,” the word for the plant in Italian has a similar root. “Rucola” means arugula, giving the name of “Rucolino,” an arugula-based amaro from the Ischia island off the coast of Naples. The Rucolino process begins with infusing a base alcohol with arugula, citrus peel, and a mix of botanicals for around 40 days. Then, producers sweeten the liqueur with sugar or syrup before letting it age. Rucolino’s flavor retains the fresh, peppery bite of arugula with bittersweet, herbaceous undertones. Much like other amari, the liqueur is traditionally consumed as a post-meal digestivo.

Sardinia: Mirto

Mirto is a liqueur made with the berries of a myrtle plant, an evergreen shrub indigenous to the Mediterranean. Some accounts suggest Mirto’s production began in Corsica and was later transported to Sardinia, now the home base of the spirit. Many of the island’s inhabitants make batches of Mirto at home for recreational consumption, and only a few professional producers exist. Making the beverage begins with steeping the berries in a high-proof neutral alcohol for up to 60 days. They then strain the liquid, separately press the fruit, and mix in the juice, the volume depending on how much they want to proof the batch down. The ensemble then goes through a final filtration process, resulting in a dark, black currant-colored spirit. The myrtle berries impart their herbal, spicy, and almost savory taste, leading into a lingering, slightly burning finish. The traditional, berry-based Mirto is known as Mirto Rosso. The island also offers Mirto Bianco, made from the less common white variety of the myrtle berries, or the leaves of the plant.

Sicily: Amaro Averna

While Sicily’s beverage scene may be better known for the wines coming from the hot, volcanic slopes of Mount Etna, the island also offers delicious local amari. The history behind Amaro Averna isn’t entirely clear, but the brand suggests monks based in Caltanissetta passed off the original recipe to Salvatore Averna, a textile merchant, in 1868. Later generations of the family continued to build the brand, expanding its popularity worldwide, and eventually turning Fratelli Averna into a corporation in 1958. The Campari Group eventually picked it up in 2014 for €103 million ($120 million) before selling it off, along with Mirto brand Zedda Piras, for €100 million ($116 million). Despite all of the switches in ownership, Amaro Averna’s production still remains faithful to the original 19th-century recipe. The blend of botanicals is a secret, but the liqueur, bottled at 29 percent ABV, brings flavors of citrus, caramel, cola, and herbs. Sicily is also home to a few other artisanal amaro brands that work with local botanicals, including Amaro dell’Etna.

title: Two Years After American Single Malt’s Ratification, the Category Is Still Finding Its Way
summary:

content:
It’s been nearly two years since the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) ratified a standard of identity for American single malt. The milestone was hailed as a victory by distillers across the country, many of whom had been petitioning the TTB for years via the American Single Malt Whiskey Commission (ASMWC). They eagerly anticipated positive outcomes: more consumer recognition, smoother paths to the shelf, higher sales.

Such hopes remain, by and large, unrealized, as the American single malt category is dealing with the same economic challenges that are depressing sales of other whiskeys. “Things are happening slower than a lot of us would like to see simply because it’s tough times out there,” says Steve Hawley, president of the AMSWC. “I wish with all my life that it didn’t take 10 years to do what we did and we had that ratification a few years earlier when boom times were still going. The timing is unfortunate but we’re not different from any other category of whiskey right now.”

A few distilleries have gone out of business, and even some of the biggest producers of American single malt are taking it on the chin. Seattle-based Westland Distillery, owned by Rémy Cointreau, lost $1 million worth of whiskey to theft last summer; although that was a matter of bad luck, the distillery also laid off multiple staff members at the beginning of the year. Diageo subsidiary Distill Ventures wound down in 2025, leading one of the distilleries in which it held a stake, Portland, Ore.’s Westward Whiskey, to file for bankruptcy. And Diageo-owned Balcones Distillery in Waco, Texas stopped production altogether in August 2025, laying off 17 staff (and with the company’s new CEO pledging significant cuts to the workforce, more layoffs wouldn’t come as a surprise).

Still, there are bright spots. News of ratification sparked interest from the media, which has drawn attention to the niche category and provided opportunities to introduce and explain it. Producers have used the official designation to push retailers and bar owners to create dedicated sections for American single malt on their shelves and menus. And whiskey aficionados who may have had questions before are now becoming dialed in to what makes American single malt distinct, especially in relation to other whiskey styles.

“We no longer get bourbon lovers coming in and saying ‘I don’t like American single malt because I don’t like peated whiskey’,” says Justin Aden, head blender at Stranahan’s, the largest American single malt brand. The misunderstanding — that American single malt would be peated, as many Scotches are — used to be common among American whiskey drinkers visiting the distillery. Aden adds that consumers also have a better understanding of the difference between a bourbon mash bill and a 100-percent malted barley whiskey. “It sounds elementary, but it was literally not on anyone’s radar before,” he says.

But what American single malt is, and what makes it distinct, remain mostly unknown outside of connoisseur circles. Even releases from major bourbon and Tennessee whiskey brands like Jim Beam, Bulleit, and Jack Daniel’s don’t seem to have moved the needle much, although Jack remains committed to style, announcing a nationwide rollout in August. “Establishing the standard was really the beginning of building the category rather than the culmination of it,” says Jason Moore, managing director at Westland. Producers aren’t giving up, but they are adapting and looking for other opportunities to establish the category, bit by bit.

Effects of Ratification

The buildup to ratification took about a decade, which sounds like a long time but was relatively quick for an agency like the TTB. The agency had gone more than 50 years without adding a new whiskey category to the books before approving the standard of identity for American single malt in December 2024. Distillers and brands were hoping that the momentum would carry over into a positive impact on sales, but few have seen that materialize.

“We had high hopes, but it’s pretty much the same struggle,” says Stephen Paul, founder of Tucson’s Whiskey Del Bac. “Bourbon is the American whiskey. That’s a tough hurdle to get over.” He notes, however, that local stores have created dedicated sections for American single malt, something the distillery has long advocated for.

The standard of identity should get some of the credit for that, Hawley says. “It helps us in some of the practical trade aspects of making and selling whiskey,” he explains, noting that it gives retailers “incentive to create a separate shelf in their store, which we’ve shown, time and time again, is critical for our producers to be able to sell it.” Official recognition by an agency of the U.S. government also helps with tasks like export reporting; before, American single malt was just lumped into the category of “other,” making it difficult to accurately track sales.

But outside of the trade, among most consumers, the standard of identity holds little meaning, and producers still have to do some amount of education about American single malt, especially as it compares to the much more familiar category of bourbon. “I do 300 educational events a year in Oregon alone. People say, ‘Oh, whiskey, that’s not bourbon.’ You have to really start from the beginning,” says Mark Stell, founder of Bird Creek, an American single malt that focuses on unique barley varieties. “They just assume whiskey is Scotch. You have to start from the basics.”

Stell adds that distribution is another key challenge for Bird Creek, as it is for many small producers. Consolidation at the middle tier, coupled with the oversaturation of brands on the retail shelf, has narrowed avenues for growth, especially in the last couple of years. “It’s a dogfight, store to store and shelf to shelf,” says Gareth Moore, CEO of Virginia Distillery Company. “We’re investing a ton in sales and marketing to have very modest growth.”

Adjusting Expectations and Strategy

As demand for American single malt has failed to keep pace with projections, distillers are responding in different ways. In Westward’s case, the bankruptcy filing allowed it to restructure and become more agile for current conditions. CEO Tom Mooney says that the brand is “bigger today than it was before bankruptcy. We actually managed to grow over the last year and a half.”

Elsewhere, single malt distillers have leaned into new products and even diversified into different spirits altogether. Virginia Distillery Company’s Courage & Conviction single malt brand, retail-priced between $80 and $120, used to make up two-thirds of sales, but Moore says that in the last couple of years its share has fallen to one-third. The balance has shifted to the distillery’s line of cask-finished single malts, which are about half the price. Moore surmises that consumers are more comfortable with trial when the initial outlay is smaller.

“We had high hopes, but it’s pretty much the same struggle. Bourbon is the American whiskey. That’s a tough hurdle to get over.”

But Virginia Distillery Company has also moved beyond just offering single malt, incorporating a subsidiary called Pound & Penny Spirits whose portfolio includes Cierto Tequila and Kinda Light Vodka Seltzer. In addition, the company recently launched The Split Barrel Project, a bourbon–single malt blend that Moore says is acting as a gateway to the other whiskeys. “Consumers like the taste and the concept as a stepping stone,” he notes. “It’s a way to get people into the category.”

Whiskey Del Bac began expanding into bourbon and rye a few years ago with its Sentinel of the Desert line, comprising bourbon and rye from MGP that’s finished with staves from the distillery’s own mesquite-smoked whiskey casks. Paul was reluctant to diversify but the move made business sense. “We always had questions: Will you ever do a rye or bourbon? We always said no because the vision was a regional American single malt,” he explains. “Then we realized that there would be a demand and, from a cost standpoint, we needed a more cocktail-friendly whiskey.”

Stranahan’s is also targeting mixology with its Blue Peak expression, a blend of 4- to 7-year-old barrels priced around $40 at retail. “We’ve seen mixologists and bartenders shocked at the versatility of it,” Aden says. “It can fool you for a bourbon or Irish whiskey in a lot of cocktails. With the price where it is, it has been a tremendous gateway to the on premise.”

Overseas Opportunity

Unsurprisingly, American single malt producers have largely focused on domestic sales, but many say that export markets present a ripe opportunity for growth — even despite the reputational damage American whiskey is suffering. One big advantage is that the category doesn’t require a preamble of explanation overseas as it does here.

“Normally in the U.S. I find we’re explaining not what we are but what we aren’t. We’re American but we’re not bourbon. We’re single malt but we’re not Scotch,” Moore says. “Then you go international and start to explain it and someone’s like, ‘No, we get it.’ Globally the taste profile for whiskey is malt. You say whiskey overseas, they think malt.” Virginia Distillery Company currently exports to countries in Asia and Europe, as well as Australia.

Exporting American single malt requires tweaking of strategy and message but producers say it’s actually easier in many ways. “It’s an entirely different selling and marketing process when you don’t have to explain the category,” Mooney says. “The consumer understands malt whiskey and you can go straight to what makes you different. You’re not category building or explaining — you’re just telling your brand story.”

Making the jump to export isn’t necessarily straightforward, though, especially in the current sociopolitical climate. Stell was recently approached by a European importer looking for American whiskey like Bird Creek but, he says, “we have an idiotic tariff situation.” He remains hopeful that he’ll be able to make it work. “If you have a decent product, there’s a call for it, no question. Overseas markets want good products and they want a range of stuff.”

Although it’s the leading producer of American single malt, Stranahan’s has focused almost exclusively on the domestic market for its 23-year history. “We’ve always had this overlying philosophy that we didn’t really want to crack the overseas market until we could come to play with double-digit age statements,” Aden says. “Because overseas, that’s what they expect.” Now that its core line includes 10- and 12-year-old whiskeys — with higher age statements to come — Stranahan’s will begin expanding into other countries over the next couple of years.

Long Runway

Even if brands find success overseas, they still need drinkers at home to embrace the category too. With whiskey of all kinds in a rough patch, there are signs that American single malt may be better positioned than many of its bourbon and rye peers. “For better or worse there was never a bubble to burst within American single malt, so there was not a precipitous fall,” Moore says. “On a very small base it continued to grow through 2025 and so that’s a good thing for us.”

But patience, and perspective, are required. Overall sales of the category are a rounding error next to the behemoth bourbon, though Aden says that “the potential that American single malt has, even if it claws just a couple percentage points of the pie, is remarkable.”

It’s a big opportunity that will take time, but can happen if drinkers come to understand and support what makes American single malt special, just as they do with bourbon. “The exciting thing now is to try to explain that you should have just as much pride in American single malt as being a unique product of our country and representing our place as you have with bourbon,” Aden says. “We’re not trying to challenge bourbon as America’s whiskey top dog. You can have both.”

Moore points to other nontraditional single malt nations as a model of what American single malt could become: well-known, respected, beloved. “If Japan can do it and India can do it,” he says, “then sure as hell we can do it.”

content:
From line cooks and expeditors to chef-owners, back-of-house employees see how a restaurant runs from the kitchen standpoint. That behind-the-scenes knowledge gives them a unique perspective and can come in handy when dining out, especially when it comes to spotting red flags in a space.

On nights out, a chef’s sense of how a restaurant is running is just as keen as their palate, and there are certain cues that instantly set off alarms. That’s why we asked cooks and operators for the biggest red flags they notice when sitting down at a restaurant. Unsurprisingly, many call out unfriendly service as a big factor in detecting shady spots, but there are some specific signs to watch out for that can be an early indicator of the quality of the meal that lies ahead.

Here are the red flags you should clock when visiting a restaurant, according to eight restaurant pros.

The biggest red flags when sitting down at a restaurant, according to chefs:

  • An unwelcoming host
  • Rushed service
  • Unhappy staff
  • Bad pacing
  • Bad energy
  • Unattentive team
  • Dirty bathroom
  • Overlooking the guest experience
  • Dirty menus
  • White wines cooled indiscriminately in an ice bucket

“Honestly, the biggest red flag can happen before I even sit down. The host stand is crucial for setting the tone of the experience. I’ve had so many interactions with hosts who seem indifferent or annoyed by my presence, which is hard to recover from. A warm, sincere greeting goes such a long way.” —John Manion, chef, El Che and Brasero, Chicago

“I instantly notice when a restaurant makes guests feel rushed, whether it is through the pace of greeting diners as they walk through the doors, the ordering process, or the speed at which courses are cleared. A good meal should have rhythm, but it should never feel like a restaurant is trying to get you in and out as fast as possible. When hospitality is rushed and not authentic, that is the biggest red flag a restaurant can have.” —Avtar Singh Walia, owner, Tamarind Tribeca, New York City

“When I’m dining in a restaurant and the staff look miserable but are plastering on a ‘happy’ face for the guest, it’s a red flag for me. Working with people always brings conflict — it’s the nature of it. But if the crew seems stuck in tension or drama, the guest-forward hospitality feels performative instead of genuine. It’s often a sign that something is off in the culture. Every customer-facing workforce experiences times like these, but the trick lies in how to move through them so we don’t get stuck there and can return to a lightness of being with each other and a work environment we all look forward to being in. The impact our internal culture has on our external hospitality is huge.” —Molly Irani, co-founder, Chai Pani Restaurant Group, author, Service Ready, Asheville, N.C.

“A big red flag when I sit down at a restaurant is timing. If the time between when I sit down, get a glass of water, and take my first bite of food is too long, I become agitated and hangry. If the time between the following courses is too long, I easily get bored — especially at a tasting menu experience, even if it’s unintentional. Overall, this could indicate a lack of service staff, attentiveness, or a sense of urgency.” —David Yoshimura, executive chef and owner, Nisei, San Francisco

“While I try to remain open-minded, there are certain things that I register. The first is the energy of the room and the people working in it: How was my party greeted? Then comes the menu: Is it clear? Then, I watch the choreography of the meal: How attentive is the team? Even the restroom tells me something: Is it clean? Ultimately, all of these observations lead me back to one question: Do I matter? Great hospitality isn’t simply about serving good food. It’s about making someone feel seen, welcomed, cared for, and genuinely valued from the moment they walk through the door until the moment they leave. The biggest red flag is when the restaurant’s priorities become obvious and the guest isn’t one of them. A restaurant can have a bad night. It can be slammed. A dish can take too long. A server can make a mistake. Those things happen. What I’m watching for is what happens around those imperfections. Do I see a team that cares, communicates, recovers, and protects the guest experience, or one that has forgotten that the guest is the reason everyone is there? That’s the red flag I notice most: Do I matter?” —Oren Cohen, general manager, The Bindery, Denver

“The biggest red flag is being handed dirty menus when I first sit down. I think that creates a very unwelcoming feeling for a guest, starting off the experience without feeling cared for. It’s hard to win a guest back after that happens!” —Charlie Mitchell, chef, Saga, NYC

“Vibes are important at a restaurant, and they can really impact your experience as a guest. Working in the industry, it’s always obvious when I sit down at a restaurant and there’s tension in the air. Happy servers and cooks — open kitchens are trending — make for better food and dining experiences. So, a big red flag for me is when staff don’t look engaged and excited, which tells me management is not creating a positive work environment.” —Chris McLaurin, chef, Lutra Cafe & Bakery, Durham, N.C.

“All the white wine indiscriminately in an ice bucket at the bar or at a service station, at least at a nicer restaurant with a pricy by-the-glass and bottle list that’s meant to impress. Properly tempered wine should be the bare minimum.” —Zach Engel, chef, Galit and Cafe Yaya, Chicago

content:
It was a celebration in NOLA’s French Quarter as the seven regional champions of Hennessy’s Pave the Way cocktail competition shared their stories of sustainability by shaking, stirring, and chatting directly with guests.

The winners included Victor Uceda-Vereau of Bar Kaiju (Miami, FL) representing the Southeast; Lauren Pellecchia of Merchant’s Club (Newport, KY) representing Northcentral; Michael McGee, Jr. of Tallboy (Oakland, CA) representing the Northwest; Joshua Bender of Fish Gaucho (Paso Robles, CA) representing the Southwest; DJ Ballard of Press Club Cocktail Bar (Washington, D.C.) representing the Northeast; Tiffany Trotter of Follies (Mobile, AL) representing the Southern; and L. Scott of Blue Crawfish Boutique Hotel (New Orleans, LA) representing Southcentral. They showed off and served their cocktails at the historic Arnaud’s restaurant, where the Pave the Way showcase took place.

Created by Another Round Another Rally and supported by legacy cognac house Hennessy, the Pave the Way program is an educational initiative and cocktail competition that aims to empower hospitality workers by giving them tools to better expand their knowledge of cognac, build their brand, and further commit to a practice of sustainability in their communities, careers, and cocktail creation.

Oakland bartender Michael McGee felt the pull to participate in Pave the Way because of its educational and mentorship components. “I’m always down for good education, and I appreciate when people make a point to share the things they’ve learned so others can run with it,” he says. McGee built his Sidekicks cocktail with Hennessy V.S.O.P, favoring the expression’s floral brightness, candied sweetness, and delicate spice to create an overall balance between complexity and mellowness.

“Hennessy has a brand legacy of luxury and aspiration. It also has a wide appeal and has created lots of opportunities for access,” he adds.

DJ Ballard of D.C. says he wanted to participate in Pave the Way to become more conscious of how to implement sustainability in his day-to-day life and career. He views sustainability practices less as a badge or brag, and more of something that needs to be done. “I think we should just find easy and seamless ways to incorporate it into our lives,” he says. It was with this ethos in mind that he created his highly dialed-in Hennessy highball called Lemonade — a cocktail intentionally easy to replicate, while still feeling elevated, using clever ways to get the most out of the lemon, pepper, and cognac in the drink.

Even with over 20 years behind the bar, Louisiana-born-and-raised Scott was prompted to apply for the program because she never wants to feel like she knows everything — a fitting echo of the Hennessy brand’s ethos of bringing things to the best possible evolution of what they can be. She says, “It challenged me to look beyond whether a cocktail simply tastes good and examine what I am actually trying to say through the glass.” One of the biggest takeaways for her was learning to understand sustainability as more than a trend or buzzword. ”For me, it became about respect and gratitude.”

This year’s inaugural Pave the Way program unfolded in three phases, with applications opening in March. Phase one began in April with the first virtual educational component on cognac followed by a second class covering sustainability. Participants were then asked to complete a multiple choice test on cognac production, the Cognac region, Maison Hennessy, and different meanings of and paths toward sustainability. Finally, they submitted one original cocktail — captured by showing their bartender skills in a video application — highlighting Hennessy and each entrant’s personal take on sustainability.

Next, phase two saw 10 semi-finalists from each region go head-to-head in a live cocktail competition in front of a panel of judges. The semi-finalists took turns putting their new knowledge and skills to practice as they built their story of sustainability in a glass in front of judges and fellow competitors.

Bender’s cocktail leaned into the fact that Hennessy V.S.O.P is a blend of several eaux de vie (an un-aged, grape-based spirit distilled in a alembic pot still) from different crus. Each eaux de vie adds character and dimension to the blend. The result is a soft, subtle, and creamier flavor profile that works brilliantly in cocktails with finer bubbles.

“I love Hennessy because there is a signature method of blending — there’s a woody, floral nose on every blend that transforms from bright, juicy fruit to degrees of vanilla, caramel, and spice on the palate,” Bender says. For his cocktail, Skin Contact, he paired specific notes from the different eaux de vie to build adjacent flavor pairings.

When asked about the value of the educational component, Miami-native Uceda was mostly inspired by the sustainability processes he learned. Uceda then put these skills into practice, where he wowed the judges with his Burbujas en été cocktail entry, a peachy-fig cocktail using Hennessy V.S that minimized food waste by being conscientious with ingredients, like using figs in multiple ways throughout the cocktail, swapping out out-of-season peaches for peach oolong, making syrup with the leftover tea, and using acid and carbonation to make the drink more shelf-stable.

“Learning about the different ways Hennessy helps communities as well as the sustainability practices and techniques like force carbonation, acid adjusting, clarification, and so much more that could and should be implemented into our bar programs was a key takeaway.”

“I was the last competitor to present my cocktail, so the nerves were real,” says former pre-school teacher-turned-bartender Pellecchia. “But the judges were so kind and supportive, it felt like I was chatting with guests at my bar.” A tribute to her daily routine, Pellecchia’s cocktail, Full Circle, focused on ways to reuse and repurpose existing ingredients, a sustainability practice at the heart of every step of Maison Hennessy’s production.

In 2020, Hennessy began trialing the use of repurposed second-generation biofuels from frying oils and leftover distillation biogases to fuel their transportation and production processes. They also work with local glass producers to collect and reuse Hennessy’s glass bottles. As a leader of sustainability in the category, the maison aims to be 100 percent powered by biofuels and recaptured carbon.

“Sustainability is built on everyday changes that are simple to implement and simple to build on,” Pellecchia says. “So I look for sustainable options that are maintainable, in both my bar and personal life.”

Her Full Circle cocktail features a coffee-banana syrup Pellecchia makes from her morning coffee grinds, leftover frozen banana peels from breakfast, and honey powder from a local honey farm. Using the rich, fruity, and nutty notes in Hennessy V.S as an anchor and to balance out the bitterness of ingredients like the rye, dark chocolate, and coffee creates a dessert-style cocktail that isn’t cloying or overly sweet, but still feels deeply indulgent.

For New Orleans local L Scott, competing live was emotional. Upon hearing her name called as the Southcentral regional winner, she cried.

“I talked about stewardship, history, and why gratitude was so important to the story of my cocktail,” she says. Scott’s Flesh & Spirit cocktail was a very personal interpretation of a Brandy Crusta, designed to pay gratitude to the idea of flesh as it applies to fruit, such as the Ugni Blanc grapes used to make Hennessy (and over 98 percent of all cognac) and the mango in the cocktail. “I looked at the skin, the flesh, and even the kernel as different parts [of the mango], and I wanted to show gratitude to the entire ingredient instead of taking the sweetest part and discarding the rest. For this cocktail, the mango is the flesh, Hennessy is the spirit — that relationship is the heartbeat of the cocktail.”

Nearby in Mobile, AL, Trotter’s first-ever cocktail competition made her a first-time winner when her name was announced as a Pave the Way regional champion. A longtime follower of Another Round Another Rally and Hennessy, Trotter felt it was the perfect competition to beef up and showcase her skills.

“Being tasked with a theme of sustainability added a layer of turning scraps into a small luxury — how I imagine Hennessy redefining their portfolio to celebrate everyday luxuries, not just the rare occasions,” she says. For her tiki-inspired Driftwood Provision cocktail, Trotter intentionally turned away from using fresh produce, instead giving new life and delicious purpose to leftover scraps from the bar’s kitchen. “Saving a bottle of cognac for a ‘special occasion’ may not be promised, so create your own reason to celebrate!”

A common thread shared by all seven regional champions was their admiration for their fellow competitors. “The best part about competition day was watching the other presentations, so many of them were mind-blowing in concept and technique,” says Trotter.

As guests walked through the doors of Arnaud’s, a symbol of NOLA hospitality and bastion of Creole cuisine since 1918, they were greeted with a live jazz band that filled the air with a lively, festive tone.

The event unfolded across a handful of Arnaud’s 14 dining rooms with guests encouraged to move at their own pace through spaces thoughtfully designed for mingling, networking, educating, and quiet connection. Although casual and convivial, the experience was as intentional as every bottle and blend of Hennessy.

Attending guests left with a beautifully designed Hennessy Pave the Way compendium book fit for display, while the seven regional champions left with core career memories and feeling empowered with new ways to implement sustainability into their work in the glass and behind the bar.

“I think this is a key purpose of the Pave the Way program,” Trotter says. “It’s to encourage people to expand their minds, and to return home with the skills and confidence to impact their local scene and create new channels of mentorship.”
